Across these domains, evolutionary innovations gave rise to new organizational configurations that incorporated earlier architectures and enabled representations to exert causal influence with increasing independence from any particular physical instantiation.RNA-based replication established stable molecular representations capable of persisting beyond individual molecular lifetimes. The advent of the genetic code separated representation from interpretation through a dedicated translational apparatus linking nucleic acid sequences to proteins. Human language redistributed representation and interpretation across socially organized communities through symbolic communication. Contemporary artificial intelligence extends this trajectory by externalizing interpretive processes into technological systems capable of learning, generating, and transforming representations. Taken together, these transitions reveal a common evolutionary dynamic in which progressively more efficient representation–interpretation systems enable representations to retain, transmit, and extend their causal influence despite continual changes in their physical instantiation.The present analysis provides a general organizational framework for understanding the evolution of representation–interpretation systems and offers a complementary perspective on major evolutionary transitions.
